video.title: He Turns Abandoned Driving Ranges Into Cash Machines

summary: Chris Koerner visits Golf Ranch in Richardson, Dallas, whose founding team (ex-Topgolf and long-time paid-ads operator) buys dated or abandoned driving ranges and modernises them. They upgraded ball and mat quality based on customer surveys, added covered bays, lights to midnight, music, string lights and a putting green, and replaced prepaid bucket cards with a $20/month Ranch Pass membership (40% off buckets); they now have 8,000 members across four sites and claim an LTV:CAC of about 10. Volume at this site went from about 3.5 million to 12 million balls a year. The key takeaway is that an old, underserved industry with a low bar can be won by listening to customers, a membership loop, loss-leader amenities and modern digital marketing; the goal is 50 sites and 100,000 members.

speakers.name: Golf Ranch founder (first name possibly Grace; full name not stated)
speakers.description: Co-founder/operator of Golf Ranch, ~15 years running paid ads; posts as Driving Range Guys

ideas.name: Buy and modernise dated driving ranges (Golf Ranch)
ideas.one_liner: Acquire run-down or abandoned driving ranges and turn them into welcoming, tech-enabled membership practice venues.
ideas.business_model: Per-bucket ball sales plus $20/month membership (Ranch Pass), light food and beverage (~15% of revenue), lessons, par-three, events.
ideas.customer: Serious golfers (ICP), plus families, first-daters, beginners and retirees who practise off-peak
ideas.problem: Driving ranges are dated, unwelcoming and stale with poor balls and mats, no tech, closed at sundown; golfers who start at Topgolf have no middle ground before real golf
ideas.offer: High-quality balls and mats, Toptracer ball-tracking bays, covered and heated/fan-cooled bays, lights to midnight, music and mood lighting, putting green, simple food, membership with perks

pricing.model: Membership plus per-bucket pricing; members get 40% off buckets
pricing.notes: First bucket free as an acquisition offer; tiered annual memberships also exist. Coffee and hot dogs cheap as loss leaders.

acquisition_channels.details: Search ads on high-intent terms like 'golf lessons near me'.

quote.text: golf lessons near me. Huge search term that driving high intent, highly qualified leads in the business
quote.speaker: Guest

acquisition_channels.details: Facebook/social ads plus content to stay top of mind with existing customers.
In-house instructors act as salespeople pushing membership and events.
Free first bucket offer to get people on site, then convert to membership.

quote.text: One of the offers that we run at all of our locations is a free first bucket
quote.speaker: Guest

ideas.delivery: Staffed physical venues: front desk, ball picker crews picking ~10 times a day plus robotic 'Roomba' pickers and auto-cleaning dispensers, groundskeeping, instructors on payroll, flat-top food.
unit_economics_claims: Members ~40% of customers; pay 40% less per bucket
LTV north of a couple hundred dollars; LTV:CAC ~10
120,000 new balls a year at Richardson at $0.50-0.70 each
Balls hit went from ~3.5M to 12M/year; 10M+ this year at the second busiest range in the US
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated overall; major costs are land/notes, buildout, Toptracer licensing, labour, water
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: not stated (acquired operating ranges generate revenue immediately; abandoned ones start 'from minus one')

acquisition.how: Paid search/social and free-bucket offers can be run largely by software and agents.

onboarding.how: Membership signup and payments can be self-serve online.

delivery.how: Physical venue: staff, grounds, picking, food and instruction; robots help with ball picking only.

support.how: On-site hospitality and front desk are human.

uk_applicability.notes: UK has many dated driving ranges and Toptracer is already common at UK ranges; weather, land costs and planning differ. Capital intensive and physical; not suited to an automated part-time founder.

risks: Very capital intensive (land, buildout, Toptracer lease)
Abandoned sites carry bad reviews to overcome

quotes.text: So, you went from three and a half balls hit per year here 2 or 3 years ago to 12 million today

quotes.text: We should maybe jump that middleman, go out and buy these ranges and do that ourselves

ideas.name: Toptracer Range licensing (Topgolf's SaaS to ranges)
ideas.one_liner: License ball-tracking bay technology to driving ranges with buildout plus a multi-year per-bay lease and upsells.
ideas.business_model: Upfront buildout bundled into a per-bay licence, multi-year monthly lease, upsell products like Toptracer Coach and app
ideas.problem: Ranges lack data and modern experience; golfers cannot see shot distance
ideas.offer: Bay hardware, wiring, data centre, app and coach software

acquisition_channels.details: Direct sales to mom-and-pop range owners, which proved hard because many owners are in their 70s and resistant.

ideas.delivery: Toptracer installs hardware and runs software; ongoing SaaS.

acquisition.how: Enterprise hardware sales to older owners is human-heavy.

uk_applicability.notes: Already deployed in UK ranges; mentioned as an existing company's model, not a replicable side hustle.

quotes.text: They soon they soon learned it's very difficult to make that sale
quotes.speaker: Guest

ideas.name: Websites and digital marketing for old-school venue owners
ideas.one_liner: Modernise websites and run digital marketing for dated local businesses like driving ranges that haven't updated since the 1990s.
ideas.customer: Old-school local business owners (e.g. driving range owners)
ideas.problem: Websites with just an address and phone in huge fonts, not mobile optimised, no digital marketing

acquisition.how: Selling to older owners needs calls/visits; UK PECR allows cold email only to limited companies, and many such venues are sole traders/partnerships.

onboarding.how: Intake forms and AI site builders.

delivery.how: AI site builders and ad tools do much of the work with checks.

support.how: Agents can handle routine change requests.

uk_applicability.notes: Works in the UK; cold outreach constrained by PECR.

quotes.text: they haven't changed their website since 1992. It's it has their address and a phone number in size 40 fonts, not optimized for mobile
quotes.speaker: Guest

ideas.name: Remote-control car ball pickup attraction for kids
ideas.one_liner: Let kids drive RC cars to collect range balls and hit for free, a memorable family attraction (spin-off of Chris's coffee shop sandpit idea).
ideas.customer: Families with children at driving ranges
ideas.problem: Need memorable reasons for families to visit; ball picking is a cost
ideas.offer: RC cars to pick up balls on the range

acquisition.how: Venue amenity, promoted via venue marketing.

quotes.text: what if we had remote control cars that kids could go pick up their own balls and then they hit balls for free

tactics.name: Survey customers, then fix the top complaints first
steps: Run customer surveys to get tangible data on where to start
Invest first in the #1 complaint (ball quality: sort balls, replace 120k/year)
Then #2 (turf/mats: buy every mat on Amazon, test, source from small distributors)
Call your best customers personally rather than relying on email surveys

quote.text: Golf walls was the number one thing that we we got back in surveys. Number two was turf quality
quote.speaker: Guest

tactics.name: Swap prepaid cards for a cancel-anytime membership
steps: Replace prepaid bucket cards with a $20/month membership
Give 40% off buckets plus member events, par-three and lesson pricing
Make it cancel anytime to suit seasonal golfers
Use the commitment to layer programming (member competitions) that drives repeat visits

quote.text: instead of prepaying for 10 buckets with one card, let's do a monthly membership model
quote.speaker: Guest

tactics.name: Engineer the first and last five minutes
steps: Make arrival memorable
Do not rent time by the hour; let people stay as long as they want so they leave satisfied
Avoid a surprise bill at exit

quote.text: the first five minutes of your visit and the last 5 minutes. That's what you remember
quote.speaker: Guest

tactics.name: Loss-leader amenities (the Costco hot dog)
steps: Build a putting green that earns nothing but draws serious golfers from 40 minutes away
Sell cheap coffee and simple food
Treat golf instruction as a loss leader and use instructors as salespeople for membership

quote.text: This is my $150 hot dog loss leader. That is like a glue to attract real golfers
quote.speaker: Guest

tactics.name: Extend revenue hours and weather-proof
steps: Add covers to bays for heat, rain and hail
Add fans and heaters
Add lights to stay open until midnight in summer
Keep a ball inventory backlog for days the outfield cannot be picked

tactics.name: Spend capex only where the customer perceives it
steps: Keep the first ~30 yards of the outfield green; leave the rest
Use shipping containers and fresh paint instead of full buildouts

quote.text: we made a decision like no, first 30 yards matters. After that, like doesn't really matter
quote.speaker: Guest

tactics.name: Site selection for expansion
steps: Prefer existing ranges people already like that need TLC over raw land
Check public golf course count and whether they have practice facilities
Check demographics, favouring families

warnings.warning: Simple does not mean easy; don't assume you can buy a range and do what the previous owner did.

quote.text: Simple doesn't necessarily mean easy
quote.speaker: Guest

warnings.warning: Topgolf-style hourly time rental and a surprise bill ruin the last five minutes and kill repeat visits.
Assuming the market was only golfers was a mistake; families and non-golfers were a much bigger market.

quote.text: I think a mistake was assuming that who our customer was at the beginning to start the business
quote.speaker: Guest

warnings.warning: Water bills and land are huge, often surprising costs.

quote.text: water bills enormous. Like we're in the grass business
quote.speaker: Guest

warnings.warning: Growing too fast on raised capital or franchising risks underperforming venues and losing standards.
Giving up on surveys or ads after one weak attempt (10% response, $100 budget) is a common mistake.

lessons.lesson: Overlooked, dated industries have a low bar: modest upgrades beat incumbents.

quote.text: It's an old dated industry. And so that was the bar was actually really low
quote.speaker: Guest

lessons.lesson: Talk to your customers; survey everyone and phone your best customers.

quote.text: People don't talk to their customers enough. I'm going to put that on my tombstone
quote.speaker: Guest

lessons.lesson: Membership converts sporadic visits into habit and unlocks events and upsells.
Identity-driven hobbies (golf, pickleball) create loyal, low-churn customers.

quote.text: Golf is kind of more of an identity for me
quote.speaker: Guest

lessons.lesson: Retention beats cheap acquisition: Topgolf's funnel is great but repeat visits are weak.

quote.text: what their issue is is getting people to come back
quote.speaker: Guest

lessons.lesson: Selling tech into old owner-operators is hard; buying the businesses and installing it yourself can capture the upside.
A converting website and strong offer matter as much as traffic.

quote.text: You know, you can drive all the traffic you want to your website. If it's not converting well, your your spend is super inefficient
quote.speaker: Guest

lessons.lesson: Give high-touch staff (instructors) a share of upside because they own the customer relationship.
Allocate limited capital where customers perceive value; skip what they don't notice.

evidence_quality.rationale: First-hand operator with specific numbers on members, pricing, LTV:CAC, costs and volume, though profit figures are not stated.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Chris promotes tkowners.com; guest promotes Golf Ranch.
